overview.title: Getting GPUs and one-line data parallelism in Keras
overview.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world
overview.section: 18.2 Scaling up model training with multiple devices
overview.main_topic: Hardware options for multi-GPU work, figure 18.2 (two four-device replicas), and enabling data parallelism with keras.distribution.DataParallel on the JAX backend
overview.central_idea: To train on several GPUs you need several GPUs: a local multi-GPU box or, more practically, a rented cloud VM. With the JAX backend, data parallelism takes one line, set_distribution(DataParallel()), placed before building the model. You can optionally pick specific devices from list_devices().
overview.importance: It is the simplest working recipe for multi-GPU training in the book. Most readers who scale up will use this one line rather than the model-parallel APIs that follow.
learning_objectives: Read figure 18.2: global batch -> local batches -> two replicas of four GPUs -> output.
Know the two practical options for getting multiple GPUs.

List available devices and restrict data parallelism to a subset.

summary:
The page finishes the sentence from p.574: if you do large-scale distributed training without **JAX**, you are making a mistake and burning far more compute (and money) than needed.

**Figure 18.2** shows the mixed layout from p.574: a **global batch** is split into two **local batches**. Each goes to a **model replica** made of four GPUs (GPU:0-3 and GPU:4-7), and the results form the **output**. (Both boxes are labelled 'Model replica 0' in print; the second should be replica 1.)

**Getting two or more GPUs.** Colab gives only one GPU, so you either:

- **build a machine** with two to eight GPUs (big power supply, CUDA drivers, cuDNN...), which is not the best option for most people, or
- **rent a multi-GPU VM** on Google Cloud, Azure or AWS, using images with preinstalled drivers. This is the best option unless you train 24/7.

The book does not give cloud VM instructions because they go out of date quickly.

**Data parallelism with JAX.** Before building your model, add one line:

`keras.distribution.set_distribution(keras.distribution.DataParallel())`

and that is all. Keras then replicates the model on every available device and splits each batch among them (synchronous training, p.573). For finer control, `keras.distribution.list_devices()` returns device names such as `"gpu:0"`, `"gpu:1"`, which you can pass to `DataParallel` to use only those devices.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Data parallelism with Keras and JAX is simple: before building your model, add one line: keras.distribution.set_distribution(keras.distribution.DataParallel()). That's it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The global distribution setting controls how variables are created (replicated on all devices) and how input batches are split along axis 0. The model and fit() code do not change.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the lowest-effort way to use all your GPUs, and the call must come before the model is created so its variables are placed correctly.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: under the hood Keras builds a 1-D DeviceMesh over all devices with a single 'batch' axis. Variables get a fully replicated layout, and data is sharded along the batch dimension. The global batch size you pass to fit() is split among devices, so it should be divisible by the number of devices.

concepts.name: Data parallelism (Keras API)
concepts.definition: keras.distribution.DataParallel replicates model variables on every device and shards input batches across them.
concepts.intuition: Turn on 'use all my GPUs' with one switch.
concepts.technical: Set globally with keras.distribution.set_distribution before model creation; supported on the JAX backend.
concepts.significance: Near-linear speedups for models that fit on one device (p.576).
concepts.misconception: That it must be called after building the model. It must be set before, so variables are created with the right layout.

concepts.name: Multi-GPU hardware options
concepts.definition: Either a local multi-GPU machine or a rented multi-GPU cloud VM.
concepts.technical: Local needs power, CUDA and cuDNN setup; cloud VMs come with preinstalled images.
concepts.significance: Determines whether you can run 18.2 at all (Colab has one GPU).
concepts.misconception: That Colab can run these examples. It offers a single GPU.

concepts.name: Replica groups (figure 18.2)
concepts.definition: Eight devices organised as two model replicas of four devices each, each replica fed a local batch.
concepts.intuition: Two teams of four, each team working on half the batch.
concepts.technical: Corresponds to a 2 x 4 mesh: data axis of size 2, model axis of size 4 (p.576-577).
concepts.significance: The standard way of combining data and model parallelism.
concepts.misconception: That the 'Output' merges the two replicas' weights. It gathers outputs; during training gradients are averaged across replicas.

code.title: Enable data parallelism on all devices
code.what_it_does: Sets the global Keras distribution to data parallelism across all available accelerators.

line_explanations.explanation: DataParallel() with no arguments uses every detected device; set_distribution makes it the global default for variable creation and data sharding.

code.inputs_outputs: No return value; changes global Keras state.
code.algorithm: Replicate variables on all devices, split each batch along axis 0, average gradients (synchronous).
code.theory_link: Implements the data parallelism of p.573.
pitfalls: Call it before building the model.
JAX backend required for the keras.distribution API as used here.
Choose a global batch size divisible by the number of devices and large enough to keep each GPU busy (p.576).

code.title: List available devices
code.what_it_does: Returns a list of device name strings such as "gpu:0", "gpu:1".

line_explanations.explanation: Queries the backend for its devices. On a CPU-only machine you get CPU devices instead.

code.theory_link: The names are used by DataParallel and DeviceMesh(devices=...).
pitfalls: Device naming depends on the backend/platform; check the actual strings returned before hard-coding them.

code.title: Data parallelism on selected devices
code.what_it_does: Restricts data parallelism to gpu:0 and gpu:1.

line_explanations.explanation: Builds a DataParallel distribution over the two named devices and sets it globally.

code.algorithm: Same as c1 with an explicit device subset.
pitfalls: In Keras 3 the device list is probably meant to be passed by keyword, DataParallel(devices=[...]), because the first positional parameter appears to be device_mesh (see review flag).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: a defensive version of the same setup
import os
os.environ['KERAS_BACKEND'] = 'jax'   # must be set before importing keras
import keras

devices = keras.distribution.list_devices()
print(devices)
keras.distribution.set_distribution(
    keras.distribution.DataParallel(devices=devices[:2])
)
# now build and fit the model as usual

deeper.title: Rent vs buy, a back-of-envelope
deeper.body: Illustration, not from the book; the prices are made-up round numbers. If an 8-GPU machine cost $200k and the equivalent cloud VM cost $25/hour, break-even would come after about 8,000 hours, nearly a year of continuous use, before counting power, cooling and staff time. This supports the book's advice: rent unless you train 24/7.

deeper.title: What DataParallel does on each step
deeper.body: Beyond the book: (1) the global batch from your dataset is split along axis 0 into one shard per device; (2) each device runs the forward and backward pass on its shard with its replica of the weights; (3) gradients are all-reduced (averaged) across devices; (4) each device applies the identical optimizer update. With JAX, all four steps are compiled into a single XLA program per device.

takeaways: Large-scale distributed training in Keras should use the JAX backend.
Colab gives one GPU; rent a multi-GPU cloud VM unless you train continuously.
Figure 18.2: a global batch split into two local batches, each processed by a four-GPU model replica.
set_distribution(DataParallel()) before building the model is all you need for data parallelism.
list_devices() returns names like "gpu:0" that you can use to restrict the devices.

questions.question: Where must keras.distribution.set_distribution(...) be called?
questions.explanation: The book says 'before building your model', because variables must be created with the distribution's layout. Calling it later would leave existing variables on a single device.

questions.question: What does keras.distribution.list_devices() return?
questions.answer: A list of device-name strings such as "gpu:0", "gpu:1".

questions.question: In figure 18.2, what is a 'local batch' and how does it relate to the global batch?
questions.answer: Each local batch is the part of the global batch sent to one model replica. With two replicas, the global batch is split in two, and each half is processed by a group of four GPUs.
questions.explanation: The figure shows two 'Local batch' arrows coming out of the 'Global batch'.

questions.question: Which hardware option does the book recommend for most people?
options: Build a workstation with eight GPUs
Rent a multi-GPU VM on a cloud provider
Use the CPU with more threads
questions.answer: Rent a multi-GPU VM on a cloud provider
questions.explanation: The book calls renting likely the best option unless you train 24/7. Building is not the best option for most people, and Colab has a single GPU. CPUs are not discussed.

questions.question: Why can a single line of configuration give multi-GPU training without changing the model or fit() code?
questions.answer: The distribution decides how variables are placed (replicated) and how input batches are split, and the JAX/XLA compiler inserts the required communication (gradient averaging). The model logic itself is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Combines the book's one-line claim with the mechanism described on p.573 and p.577.

questions.question: How many model replicas does figure 18.2 show, and which GPUs belong to each?
questions.answer: Two replicas: GPU:0-GPU:3 and GPU:4-GPU:7 (both are printed as 'Model replica 0', but the second is replica 1).

questions.question: Do you know how you would run this on a cloud VM: which backend environment variable to set and which line to add?
questions.answer: Set KERAS_BACKEND=jax before importing Keras, then call keras.distribution.set_distribution(keras.distribution.DataParallel()) before building the model.
questions.explanation: If unsure, revisit the 'Using data parallelism with JAX' subsection.
